headline: SpaceX Sells $32 Billion of AI Chip Debt at Yields Topping 8%
author: Brian Smith, Davide Barbuscia and Caleb Mutua

paragraphs.text: (Bloomberg) -- SpaceX sold $32 billion of bonds to fund its purchase of artificial intelligence chips on Thursday, in a complicated and relatively high-yielding transaction that may serve as a model for a wave of similar financings to come.
Most Read from Bloomberg

The debt offering was designed to keep the borrowing off SpaceX's balance sheet, and is part of a more than $40 billion financing that also includes bank loans. The deal will effectively allow SpaceX to buy Nvidia Corp. chips that the rocket, satellite and artificial intelligence company will lease for about five years.

The debt was sold on Thursday in three parts, according to people with knowledge of the matter. Goldman Sachs Group Inc. and Apollo Global Management Inc. ran the transaction, the people said, asking not to be identified as they're not authorized to speak publicly. Representatives for the firms and SpaceX didn't respond to requests for comment.

The biggest of the three portions sold on Thursday, about $25.2 billion of Class A3 notes, were priced at a yield of 8.259%, a relatively high level for an investment grade security. The average US high-grade note yielded 5.95% on Thursday, according to Bloomberg index data. The bonds also offered a premium over SpaceX's existing debt from its June offering, which tanked in the secondary market after the securities started trading.

Investors had already committed to buy about $26 billion of the bonds earlier, with the final $6 billion, part of the Class A3, offered on Thursday. Many of the securities were sold to investors that focus on blue-chip corporate bonds.

The chips will be bought through a special-purpose vehicle known as Saturn Funding Trust and managed by an Apollo-backed entity. SpaceX is leasing from the vehicle, and has committed to make the payments even if the equipment fails or there's an extraordinary occurrence like a natural disaster, known as a "force majeure" event.

The financing structure is expected to help SpaceX maintain investment-grade credit ratings — a critical competitive advantage for many of the biggest companies competing in the AI space, because it allows them to borrow more money, faster.

Bret Johnsen, SpaceX's chief financial officer, highlighted the company's "strong investment-grade balance sheet" on a conference call with investors after posting results last month. SpaceX sold $86.2 billion of stock in a June initial public offering and priced $25 billion of high-grade corporate bonds days later.

Companies will need some $1.5 trillion to pay for computer chips driving the artificial intelligence buildout, and deals to finance these purchases will probably become more commonplace, Scott Goodwin, co-founder of hedge fund manager Diameter Capital Partners, said at a conference this week.
"It's a new asset class," Goodwin said.

Tech companies are tapping all corners of capital markets to raise the trillions of dollars needed for data centers and other AI infrastructure, testing the depths of investor demand and risking indigestion. Thursday's debt sale came one day after AI giant Anthropic PBC completed the largest-ever initial public offering, exceeding SpaceX's own IPO.

After investors lost money on SpaceX's earlier unsecured bond offering, "we've definitely had concern from clients that are very skeptical about how is this deal going to go," said Davis Hebert, head of technology, media and telecom at research firm CreditSights. "I do think that's why the pricing on this is really wide to try and attract participation for more traditional investors."

The latest deal structure was complex for investment-grade investors to analyze, particularly as financing deals tied to AI graphics processing units, or GPUs, are relatively new, with investors still assessing risks related to the lifecycle and valuation of the chips.
BlackRock Inc., Goldman Sachs Asset Management and KKR & Co. accounts were among the anchor investors in the latest transaction, the company said in October.

SpaceX is raising a total of more than $40 billion through the broader transaction, which includes the bonds priced Thursday and a senior secured loan. The debt package will be used to pay for about $47.3 billion of GPU equipment, namely Nvidia's latest Rubin chips, earlier documents showed. Delivery of the chips is expected to begin in January.
--With assistance from Carmen Arroyo, Dan Wilchins and Scott Carpenter.
